content: Improving adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) through mutual support and education benefits both individuals living with HIV and their partners, regardless of their HIV status. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that key populations, including people who inject drugs (PWID), their partners, and prisoners, should be offered HIV testing services (HTS) at least annually, with more frequent testing based on risk behaviors. Community-based HTS is essential for reaching PWID who are unlikely to visit healthcare facilities for HIV testing. Services led by trained lay providers, including peer-based interventions, play a critical role in early detection and linking PWID, especially adolescents, to necessary care and treatment services. To enhance access to HIV testing, community-based HTS should be provided in settings that are convenient and acceptable to PWID, including adolescents, without requiring parental or guardian consent. Informed consent must always be obtained before conducting HIV testing, and confidentiality must be strictly maintained for all key populations, including those in detention or incarceration. Confidentiality extends beyond test results to include personal information such as sexual behavior and drug use. Disclosure of HIV status to sexual partners, supportive family members, or healthcare workers should only occur with the consent of the individual being tested. Healthcare workers providing HTS require specialized training to ensure the confidentiality of medical records. Accurate test results and quality assurance in both testing and counseling are critical. ART should be initiated in all tuberculosis (TB) patients living with HIV, including those with drug-resistant TB, regardless of CD4 count. Anti-TB treatment should begin first, followed by ART within the first eight weeks of TB treatment. For patients with CD4 counts below 50 cells/mm³, ART should be started within the first two weeks of TB treatment initiation. Co-existing conditions such as hepatitis B or C, alcohol dependence, active drug use, or mental health issues should not be barriers to initiating HIV or TB treatment. Efavirenz is the preferred non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor for patients starting ART while on anti-TB treatment. ART should be provided and maintained in eligible individuals living with HIV at care settings where opioid substitution therapy (OST) is available. Routine co-trimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT) should be administered to all HIV-infected patients with active TB, regardless of CD4 count, as it prevents secondary bacterial and parasitic infections. CPT is a simple, cost-effective intervention that can be safely administered alongside ART. HIV and TB programs, as well as governmental and non-governmental healthcare providers, must ensure that PWID with TB who are diagnosed with HIV are offered ART as early as possible, ideally at the same location where they receive TB treatment and OST. Effective referral systems are an alternative but require proactive follow-up and consideration of the patient’s ability to manage associated costs and time. Patients undergoing co-treatment for TB, HIV, and drug dependence should be closely monitored for side effects, including TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, which is common but usually self-limiting. Preventive therapy with CPT should be integrated into HIV chronic care for TB patients living with HIV. Evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) demonstrates that CPT reduces mortality, morbidity, and hospitalization rates without significant adverse events, even in areas with high antibiotic resistance. HIV prevention for PWID should include access to sterile injecting equipment through needle and syringe programs (NSPs), consistent and correct condom use with compatible lubricants, and periodic screening for asymptomatic sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) should be available to all eligible PWID on a voluntary basis after potential HIV exposure. Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) containing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate should be offered to individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection as part of a combination prevention approach. HIV prevention efforts must address the changing needs of PWID throughout their lifetime. Sharing injecting equipment remains the greatest risk factor for HIV transmission among PWID, followed by sexual transmission. Comprehensive prevention strategies should include NSPs, OST, STI services, condom distribution, PEP, PrEP, targeted education, and voluntary medical male circumcision in high-prevalence settings. HIV and TB programs should collaborate closely with prison health services to prevent therapy interruptions during incarceration. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and community-led organizations can facilitate these linkages. Including PWID in the design, implementation, and evaluation of prevention programs is critical for their success. NSPs should ensure the distribution of sterile injecting equipment, including low dead-space syringes, and establish safe disposal systems to reduce community contamination and needle-stick injuries. OST with methadone or buprenorphine is the most effective pharmacological treatment for opioid dependence and reduces HIV and viral hepatitis transmission by decreasing injecting drug use. OST also supports adherence to ART and TB treatment when provided in adequate doses and for sufficient durations. STI prevention, screening, and treatment should be integrated into comprehensive HIV care for PWID. Syndromic management of symptomatic STIs should be provided in the absence of laboratory tests, following national guidelines. Male and female condoms, along with wateror silicone-based lubricants, should be promoted to reduce the risk of HIV and STI transmission. PEP should be prescribed following potential HIV exposure, with a 28-day course of at least two antiretroviral drugs, preferably three, as per WHO guidelines. PrEP should be offered to individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection, defined as an incidence greater than 3 per 100 person-years without PrEP. High adherence to PrEP has demonstrated significant efficacy in preventing HIV transmission through sexual exposure, though its effectiveness in preventing transmission via shared injection equipment remains unproven. Harm reduction services, including access to sterile injection equipment and drug dependence treatment, remain central to preventing HIV and other diseases among PWID.
